claims.text: The baseline is bulk equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi with a single-phase FCC structure.
The equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi baseline has lower lattice distortion than the proposed modified alloy.
Replacing a small fraction of an element with an element of distinctly larger atomic radius will increase atomic-size mismatch.
Increased atomic-size mismatch enhances local lattice distortion in CoCrFeMnNi.
Enhanced local lattice distortion promotes concurrent deformation-twin nucleation and dislocation slip.
Local lattice distortion lowers the nucleation barriers for both twins and dislocations.
Synergistic coordination of dislocation activity and deformation twinning distributes or partitions strain.
The coordinated twinning and slip suppress plastic instability and delay necking.
The proposed mechanism provides simultaneous strength and ductility.
The modified alloy will have a higher deformation-twin density than equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
The modified alloy will develop a more spatially distributed dislocation network than the baseline.
The modified alloy will have greater strain-rate sensitivity than the baseline.
The modified alloy will exhibit delayed necking relative to the baseline.
The modified alloy will achieve higher uniform elongation at comparable yield strength.
The mechanism is expected to apply to bulk, single-phase CoCrFeMnNi under room-temperature tensile loading when composition changes are small enough to avoid secondary phases.
Secondary phases or segregation could cause observed mechanical changes independently of the intended lattice-distortion mechanism.

Room-temperature tensile testing across strain rates with in situ microscopy can compare twin nucleation, dislocation activity, necking, and mechanical response between the baseline and modified alloys.
Failure to obtain statistically significant increases in twin density, delayed necking, and strain-rate sensitivity would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis is explicitly bounded to single-phase alloys without secondary-phase formation, and the uncertainty field treats secondary phases as a confounder. The falsification rule nevertheless says that detecting secondary phases would refute the hypothesis, although such detection would instead place the experiment outside the stated boundary and prevent a clean test of the proposed mechanism.
